children: Directors in Africa have had to navigate changing environmental, political and business landscapes, and, therefore, treat sustainability as a core business consideration. They have developed game plans that show what effective strategic sustainability governance looks like in the next decade.

The risks that defined those experiences are real. Kenyan firms lose an average of 11 days a year to power outages (World Bank Enterprise Surveys), self-generated back-up power can cost businesses up to three times grid rates (Energy for Growth Hub), transport bottlenecks cost East African economies 1.7-2.8 percent of GDP (Overseas Development Institute) and the Horn of Africa has just endured its worst drought in more than four decades.

For a director, these are not footnotes in a sustainability report, but underpin the company’s margin, jobs, investor confidence and ability to operate. They force the question every board must ask: can the business survive in this volatile changing environment?Faced with these realities, African regulators and MPs are also acting. South Africa’s King codes pioneered “integrated thinking” years before global frameworks caught up, and King V – launched in October 2025 – embeds sustainability as a core governance principle.

Nigeria is among the first countries to adopt the ISSB’s global disclosure standards, with dozens of entities under way. Kenya is moving towards mandatory ISSB-aligned sustainability disclosures for listed companies and other public-interest entities. The continent so often described as catching up on disclosure is, in fact, helping set the global standard when it comes to next-gen sustainability governance.

These forces have led to innovation. African Risk Capacity, born of the AU, pioneered sovereign parametric insurance that pays out automatically when drought thresholds are breached. Morocco’s Noor complex ranks among the largest concentrated solar installations on Earth. Pay-as-you-go solar, financed over mobile money, has brought power to millions of off-grid households and is being replicated across emerging markets. Mission 300, backed by 48 governments through the Dar es Salaam Energy Declaration, aims to connect 300 million people to electricity by 2030, while platforms like Africa50 and the Private Infrastructure Development Group use blended finance to draw in capital. These are not adaptations of someone else’s playbook; they are African-designed models built on access, resilience and affordability.

It is important that African boards keep pushing forward. They are positioned to serve as key coordinators by bringing together governments, the business community and public investors to shore up the infrastructure every economy depends on. Energy is the natural starting point, but the same logic extends to health, safety, water access and infrastructure more broadly.

None of it should be entirely outsourced to foreign capital and distant priorities. Boards should consider:Recruiting directors with real energy, infrastructure or climate expertise, so strategic, customised sustainability judgment sits at the table.
Routing sustainability through the risk, finance and strategy committees, where it shapes capital allocation and becomes ingrained in other business operations.
Engaging governments, regulators and investors directly on the policy certainty and risk mitigation that large-scale infrastructure investment requires.

Africa is writing its unique sustainability script and has no shortage of raw material to draw on– renewable energy assets and a young and growing population capable of supplying the labour and consumer demand needed to help propel the next era of growth. That growth depends in large part on coordination between key local and international players to create opportunities to invest in whole systems. This would help bring Africa’s pension and insurance sectors to the table. With access to more than $777 billion in capital, their involvement is critical to help turn this potential into long-term security.

Karina Funk of US-based investment management firm highlights that “investors are examining companies’ sustainability strategies and implementation practices when making asset allocation decisions. Boards increasingly need to demonstrate a clear understanding of how sustainability-related issues affect their business operations and have appropriate processes to maintain a long-term focus on those challenges”.
African boards will serve as key figures in writing the next chapter that brings these pieces together and helps their businesses survive.
The famous saying, “The best way to predict the future is to create it”, can apply to well-structured boards that cast the vision and keep sustainability at the centre of the board agenda.
Dr Herta von Stiegel is founder & CEO of Ariya Capital Group; Daniel Weber is a communications consultant
